title: Compressive Dressing and Pharyngocutaneous Fistula After Primary Total Laryngectomy
official: Impact of Compressive Dressing on the Risk of Pharyngocutaneous Fistula After Primary Total Laryngectomy: A Multicenter Retrospective Observational Study
summary: Pharyngocutaneous fistula (PCF) is one of the most feared complications after total laryngectomy. A compressive neck dressing is often applied after surgery to try to prevent it, but there is no consensus on whether it works or how long it should be kept, and practice varies widely between centers. This multicenter, retrospective, observational study compares the rate of PCF in adult patients with laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma who underwent primary total laryngectomy with direct closure of the hypopharyngeal mucosa and who did or did not receive a postoperative compressive dressing. It also examines whether the duration of the dressing affects the risk of fistula and how fistulas were managed in the two groups. All data are collected from existing medical records; no additional treatment or examination is performed.
conditions: Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Larynx
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx treated with primary total laryngectomy
* Primary closure of the hypopharyngeal mucosa
* Age 18 years or older
* Informed consent to study participation and to personal data processing
* Availability of data on comorbidities, laboratory parameters, and postoperative management

Exclusion Criteria:

* Salvage total laryngectomy
* Previous radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy to the head and neck
* Previous open surgery of the pharyngolaryngeal region
* Reconstruction with a free or pedicled flap (inlay or onlay)
